'''Andrew Browder''' (January 8, 1931 – March 24, 2019) was an American mathematician at [[Brown University]].<ref name="brown">{{cite web|url=https://www.math.brown.edu/faculty/browder.html|title=Andrew Browder &#124; Department of Mathematics &#124; Brown University|website=math.brown.edu|accessdate=16 October 2020|archive-date=31 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180831035446/https://www.math.brown.edu/faculty/browder.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name=Tribute-Browder>{{cite web |title=Andrew Browder |publisher=Tribute Archive |url=https://www.tributearchive.com/obituaries/22337301/andrew-browder |date=22 April 2019 |access-date=14 January 2023}}</ref>

==Early life==
Andrew Browder was born in [[Moscow]], Russia, where his father [[Earl Browder]], an American communist from Kansas, United States, was living and working for a period. His mother was Raisa Berkman, a Russian Jewish woman from St. Petersburg. His brothers were [[Felix Browder]] (older), also born in Moscow, and [[William Browder (mathematician)|William Browder]] (younger). All three brothers had careers in mathematics. Their father returned to the United States in the early 1930s, bringing his family with him. The senior Browder became head of the [[Communist Party USA]]. He ran for US president in 1936 and 1940.<ref name=Tribute-Browder/>

==Career==
Browder traced his interest in mathematics to 1955 when he was a private at [[Fort Dix]] and [[Eisenhower]] offered early release to servicemen entering [[graduate school]]. He studied at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. For two years he was a Miller Fellow at [[University of California, Berkeley]] and also studied at [[Aarhus, Denmark]]. As for teaching, "I taught well over one hundred courses, some of which I found interesting and enjoyable, some pretty depressing, most somewhere in between. The students had parallel experiences."<ref name=Tribute-Browder/><ref>M. Cook & R. C. Gunning (2013) [https://muse.jhu.edu/chapter/1203335 Andrew Browder], ''Mathematicians: An Outer View of an Inner World'', pages 124,5, [[Princeton University Press]] via [[Project MUSE]]</ref>

==Personal life==

Browder married and had three children including Laura Browder, professor of American Studies at the [[University of Richmond]].<ref name=Tribute-Browder/><ref>

The analytic nature of the game of [[chess]] enthralled Browder early on: "My own main sport was always chess. My father taught me the game when I was six, a friend of the family gave me a chess book when I was eleven or twelve, and after that I was hooked."{{cn|date=January 2023}}

== Death ==
Andrew Browder died age 88 on March 24, 2019.<ref name=Tribute-Browder/>

==Works==

In 1969 Browder published ''Introduction to Function Algebras''. "The author develops much of the general theory of [[function algebra]]s and then applies it in the last two chapters to the theory of [[Padé approximation|rational approximation]] in the plane, and to finding analytic structure in the spectrum of a [[Dirichlet algebra]]."<ref>H. S. Bear [[Mathematical Reviews]] #0246125</ref>

In 1996 he published an upper-level [[textbook]] ''Mathematical Analysis'' for well-motivated students having a background of [[calculus]] and [[linear algebra]]. Four topics are encompassed by the text: single-variable theory, [[topology]] and [[function space]]s, [[measure theory]] and [[Lebesgue integration]], and [[function of several variables|functions of several variables]].<ref>[[Robert G. Bartle]] ''Mathematical Reviews'' #1411675</ref>

In 2000 Browder published his article "Topology in the Complex Plane", which described the [[Brouwer fixed point theorem]], the [[Jordan curve theorem]], and [[Alexander duality]].<ref>A. Browder (2000) "Topology in the Complex Plane", ''[[American Mathematical Monthly]]'' 107(5): 393–401 {{mr|id=1763391}}</ref>

With Hiroshi Yamaguchi, Browder wrote "A variation formula for harmonic modules and its application to several complex variables".<ref>A. Browder & Hiroshi Yamaguchi (1994) [https://www.projecteuclid.org/euclid.hmj/1206127923 A variation formula for harmonic modules and its application to several complex variables], ''[[Hiroshima Mathematical Journal]]'' 24(3): 493–520 via [[Project Euclid]]</ref>
